hints: A shortest cycle can be exposed by breadth-first search from one of its vertices.
A non-parent edge joining two visited vertices gives a cycle candidate.
Run BFS from every vertex and minimize distance[u]+distance[v]+1.
analogy: Growing distance layers from every starting point reveals a shortcut connecting two branches.
example: A triangle has a cycle of length 3, the smallest possible in a simple graph.
algorithm: For each vertex run BFS, recording distances and parents. For every edge to an already visited vertex that is not the BFS parent edge, consider distance[u]+distance[v]+1. Print the smallest candidate over all searches, or -1 if none exists.
correctness: Every non-tree edge supplies a closed walk containing a cycle no longer than its candidate. Starting BFS on a shortest cycle also yields a candidate no longer than that cycle, so the global minimum equals the girth.
complexity: For n vertices and m edges, O(n(n+m)) time and O(n+m) space.
